# Stable Matching with Deviators and Conformists<sup>∗</sup>

**Abstract**

In the Stable Marriage and Stable Roommates problems, there are inherent trade- offs between the size and stability of solutions. While in the former problem, a stable matching always exists and can be found efficiently using the Gale-Shapley algorithm, the existence of a stable matching is not guaranteed in the latter problem, but can be determined efficiently using Irving’s algorithm. However, the computation of matchings that minimise the instability, either due to the presence of constraints on the size of the matching or due to restrictive preference cycles, gives rise to a collection of infamously intractable _almost-stable matching_ problems.

In practice, however, not every agent is able or likely to initiate deviations caused by blocking pairs. Suppose we knew, for example, due to a set of requirements or estimates based on historical data, which agents are likely to initiate deviations - the _deviators_ - and which are likely to comply with whatever matching they are presented with - the _conformists_. Can we decide efficiently whether a matching exists in which no deviator is blocking, i.e., in which no deviator has an incentive to initiate a deviation? Furthermore, can we find matchings in which only a few deviators are blocking?

We characterise the computational complexity of this question in bipartite and non- bipartite settings. Surprisingly, these problems prove intractable in very strong ways. On the positive side, we identify polynomial-time and fixed-parameter tractable cases (with respect to the number of deviators and the preference list length), providing novel algorithms for problems where stability cannot be fully guaranteed, and resolving some open cases from the literature along the way.

**Keywords** Stable Marriage, Stable Roommates, Almost-Stable Matching, Parametrised Com- plexity, Fairness, Efficient Algorithm

## 1 Introduction

The two foundational stable matching problems Stable Marriage (smi) and Stable Roommates (sri) were first studied by Gale and Shapley [21]. In the former problem, we are given two disjoint sets of agents, traditionally referred to as men and women, with ordinal preferences over each other. In the latter problem, agents are part of just one set and express preferences over other agents in the same set. Agents may express incomplete preferences, deeming some possible partners unacceptable. Now, we seek a _matching_ consisting of disjoint pairs of mutually acceptable agents. In practice, not all matchings are equally good - usually, fairness and robustness requirements apply. For example, and for the purpose of this paper, we mainly consider _stable matchings_, that is, matchings that do not admit any _blocking pairs_ consisting of mutually acceptable agents that prefer each other to their current partners (or remain unmatched). This requirement underpins many real-world allocation tasks, such as matching junior doctors (so-called residents) to hospital positions [35], university students to dormitory rooms [2], and network users to communication channels [4]. Much of the literature focuses on the design of efficient algorithms for centralised matching schemes for such problems [38]. A key natural question is the following.

**Question:** Does there exist a matching in which no agent is blocking?

Gale and Shapley [21] gave an affirmative answer to this question for the smi setting and provided an efficient algorithm to find such a stable matching. However, in the sri setting, the existence of such a matching is not guaranteed (see [30] for an extensive structural overview), though Irving [34] presented an efficient algorithm to decide the existence of a stable matching in this setting.

However, to make stable matchings useful in practice, two key challenges need to be overcome. First, when allowing agents to express incomplete preferences over agents, there can be a significant trade-off between the stability and the size of a matching, as, even in the smi setting, stable matchings might not be maximum-cardinality matchings [8]. Furthermore, as already highlighted above, stable matchings might not exist at all in the sri setting [23]. The following question arises.

**Question:** Does there exist a _maximum-cardinality_ matching in which no agent is blocking?

Gale and Sotomayor [22] (for the smi setting) and Gusfield and Irving [30] (for the sri setting) observed that the set of matched agents is identical in all stable matchings when preferences are assumed to be strict (an important assumption we make throughout this paper). Consequently, all stable matchings have the same size. However, stable matchings might be significantly smaller than maximum-cardinality matchings, and real-world applications usually require as many agents to be matched as possible. Bertsimas and Gao [6], for example, recently noted that even relaxing the stability requirement by a little bit can give significant benefits with regard to the size of the achievable matchings. One way to do so is to seek a maximum- cardinality matching that is "as stable as possible". Eriksson and Häggström [17] reviewed different measures of instability and concluded that, among these measures, the number of blocking pairs is often the most useful measure of instability [38].

However, are all agents really likely to identify and act on opportunities to deviate in practice? For example, in a school choice or job market setting, are all schools, companies, and applicants equally likely to reach out to better potential partners post-matching to identify blocking pairs? Naturally, the answer in many practical scenarios is not necessarily - some agents simply do not have the capability, resources, or incentives to detect a beneficial opportunity, while others do. For example, a well-staffed hospital may have the means to follow up on better applicants to check if they have an incentive to come to this hospital, or applicants with more time on their hands may have the means to call up better places they applied to to enquire if they have an incentive to take them. Still, other agents who are unlikely to initiate deviations themselves may still deviate when someone else reaches out to them about a beneficial<tbc>

<tbc>deviation opportunity. Thus, in such settings, there may be less of a practical need to minimise the instability of these agents. Specifically, in situations where full stability is not achievable, for example due to the presence of additional constraints on the size of the matching, or due to restrictive preference cycles, it may be feasible to simply enforce that no _deviator_ (i.e., the agents that are likely to deviate when given a beneficial opportunity) has a beneficial opportunity to deviate, while placing no such requirement on the _conformists_ (i.e., the agents that are unlikely to initiate deviations). In this paper, we focus on the following natural question and its extensions across a variety of different settings.

**Question:** Does there exist a _desirable_ matching in which no _deviator_ is blocking?

### 1.1 Our Contributions

In this paper, we outline the computational landscape surrounding the computation of (maximum- cardinality) matchings that minimise the instability of a given subset of _deviator agents_ in terms of their numbers and sets of blocking pairs. Unfortunately, we derive strong intractability results: even deciding whether there exists a matching (maximum-cardinality matching) in which no deviator agent is in any blocking pair is NP-complete for sri (respectively smi). On the positive side, we present efficient parametrised algorithms (with respect to the number of deviators and the preference list length) and polynomial-time algorithms for instances with short preference lists. We also extend our results to the minimisation of blocking deviator agents and resolve some further open questions from the literature.

### 1.2 Structure of the Paper

In Section 2, we give formal definitions and discuss relevant related work. Deviator-stability in terms of blocking pairs is introduced and investigated in Section 3, followed by parametrised algorithms in Section 4. In Section 5, we extend the results to an alternative blocking agent perspective. Section 6 contains flexible, efficient algorithms for instances with very short lists that can minimise blocking pairs involving deviator agents, or the number of blocking deviators. In Section 7 we resolve some further open cases from the literature. Finally, we summarise new and known complexity results in  1 and pose open questions in Section 8.

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Formal Definitions

In Section 1, we introduced the smi and sri problems informally. Now, we will provide formal definitions of these problem instances that apply throughout this paper.

**Definition 2.1** (sri Instance)**.** _A_ Stable Roommates with Incomplete Lists (sri) instance, _denoted by_ \(I=(A,\succ)\)_, consists of a set of_ \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) _agents A_={_a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub>_,...,a<sub>n</sub>_} _and a tuple_ \(\succ\) _of n_ preference rankings \(\succ_i\) _(where i is the index of corresponding agent a<sub>i</sub>) over a subset of A_\\{_a<sub>i</sub>}. We say that a<sub>i</sub>_ prefers _a<sub>j</sub> to a<sub>k</sub> if_ \(a_j\succ_ia_k\)_. If_ \(a_j\succ_ia_k\) _or j=k, we will write_ \(a_j\unknown_ia_k\)_. Two agents a<sub>i</sub> and a<sub>j</sub> are referred to as_ acceptable _if they appear in each other’s preference rankings. Throughout, we assume that acceptability is symmetric._

Note that any sri instance \(I=(A,\succ)\) can be modelled as a graph _G_=(_A,E_), where every agent is a vertex and every acceptable pair of agents induces an edge in _E_. From hereon, _G_ is referred to as the _acceptability graph_ of _I_. If _G_ is isomorphic to a complete graph on |_A_| vertices, then we say that _I_ has _complete preferences_. Otherwise, we say that _I_ has _incomplete preferences_. The restriction of sri instances to instances that have bipartite acceptability graphs is the class of Stable Marriage with Incomplete Lists (smi) instances. Given a bipartition of _A_ into mutually exclusive but collectively exhaustive subsets _A_<sub>1</sub> and _A_<sub>2</sub>, we say that an smi<tbc>

instance has complete preferences (with respect to this bipartition) if its acceptability graph is isomorphic to the complete bipartite graph on |_A_<sub>1</sub>|,|_A_<sub>2</sub>| vertices.

Throughout, we define matchings and associated concepts as follows.

**Definition 2.2** (Matchings)**.** _Let_ \(I=(A,\succ)\) _be an_ sri _(or_ smi_) instance. Then a_ matching _M of I is a set consisting of (unordered) disjoint pairs of agents. For any pair_ \(\{a_i,a_j\}\in M\)_, we refer to a<sub>j</sub> as the_ partner_, denoted by M(a<sub>i</sub>), of a<sub>i</sub>, and vice versa. If there exists some a<sub>j</sub> such that_ \(\{a_i,a_j\}\in M\)_, then we refer to a<sub>i</sub> as_ matched _in M. Otherwise, we refer to a<sub>i</sub> as_ unmatched _and denote M(a<sub>i</sub>_)=_a<sub>i</sub>._

_The set of all matchings of I is given by_ M_. A_ maximum-cardinality matching _is a matching M of I such that, for any other_ \(M'\in\mathcal{M}\)_, it is true that_ \(|M|\ge|M'|\)_. The set of all maximum-cardinality matchings is denoted by_ M<sup>+</sup>_. Furthermore, maximum-cardinality matchings are_ perfect _if every agent is matched (to someone other than themselves). The set of perfect matchings (which might be empty) is denoted by_ M_<sup>p</sup>._

We formalise the classical concept of stability below.

**Definition 2.3** (Stability)**.** _Given an_ sri _(or_ smi_) instance_ \(I=(A,\succ)\) _and a matching M of I, a pair of distinct agents_ {_a<sub>i</sub>,a<sub>j</sub>_} _is a_ blocking pair _of M if_ \(a_i\succ_jM(a_j)\) _and_ \(a_j\succ_iM(a_i)\)_. The set of blocking pairs of M is denoted by bp(M). Given an agent a<sub>i</sub> and a matching M, we can restrict the set of blocking pairs to those containing a<sub>i</sub>, the set of which we denote by bp<sub>a<sub>i</sub></sub>(M). Finally, we refer to a<sub>i</sub> as a_ blocking agent _if_ \(bp_{a_i}(M)\neq\emptyset\)_. The set of all blocking agents of a matching M is denoted by ba(M)._

Any matching that has an empty set of blocking pairs is referred to as _stable_. Any other matching is referred to as _unstable_. Furthermore, we refer to an instance that admits at least one stable matching as _solvable_, and as _unsolvable_ otherwise.

We also assume knowledge of the following "almost-stable" matching problem that aims to minimise the number of blocking pairs, first formalised by Abraham et al. \[1\].

In the introduction, we highlighted already that even a solvable instance might not admit a stable matching which is simultaneously a maximum-cardinality matching. Given the practical importance of large matchings, another key almost-stable matching problem is to find a maximum-cardinality matching that minimises the number of blocking pairs it admits \[8\], which we define below.

To establish key computational complexity results in this paper, we will refer to the decision problem (2,2)-e3-sat, which is a restriction of the classical Satisfiability problem (sat), that is known to be NP-complete, see Berman et al. \[5\]. The problem is defined as follows.

MinBP-AlmostStable-sri
Input: sri instance I.
Output: A matching M of I such that |bp(M)| = minM' \in\mathcal{M}|bp(M')|.

MinBP-AlmostStable-Max-smi
Input: smi instance I.
Output: A maximum-cardinality matching M of I such that |bp(M)| = minM' \in\mathcal{M}^+|bp(M')|.

(2,2)-e3-sat
Input: Boolean formula B in CNF, where every clause contains exactly three (distinct) literals, and every variable occurs exactly twice unnegated and twice negated.

This rather restrictive definition of classical sat has a nice structure. For example, the following formula is a yes-instance: \(B=(V_1\vee V_2\vee V_3)\wedge(\bar{V}_1\vee\bar{V}_2\vee\bar{V}_3)\wedge(V_1\vee\bar{V}_2\vee V_3)\wedge(\bar{V}_1\vee V_2\vee\bar{V}_3)\), as the truth assignment setting _V_<sub>1</sub> to true and _V_<sub>2</sub> and _V_<sub>3</sub> to false satisfies _B_.

## 2.2 Related Work

Abraham et al. \[1\] established that the problem MinBP-AlmostStable-sri is NP-hard even for complete preference lists, and Biró et al. \[7\] extended this intractability result to instances where every agent has a preference list of length at most 3. The first set of authors also proved that it is NP-hard to approximate MinBP-AlmostStable-sri within any \(n^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) (for any \(\varepsilon>0\), where _n_ is the number of agents), and Chen et al. \[11\] proved that the problem is W\[1\]-hard with respect to the parameter \(min_{M\in\mathcal{M}}|bp(M)|\) even when preference lists are of length at most 5.

For smi, Biró, Manlove and Mittal \[8\] studied the trade-off between matching size and stability from a computational complexity perspective. They showed that MinBP-AlmostStable- Max-smi (and a similar problem minimising the number of blocking agents) is NP-hard even to approximate within \(n^{1-\varepsilon}\) (for any \(\varepsilon>0\)) \[8\]. Later, Hamada et al. \[31\] strengthened this result to hold even in the presence of short preference lists of length at most 3. In contrast, for preference lists of length at most 2, Biró, Manlove and Mittal \[8\] showed that MinBP- AlmostStable-Max-smi (and the minimisation of blocking agents) is polynomial-time solvable. However, MinBP-AlmostStable-Max-smi is W\[1\]-hard even for a variety of combined parameters, which was studied extensively by Gupta et al. \[28\]. Recently, Chen, Roy and Simola \[12\] proved in a preprint that it is W\[1\]-hard (with respect to the optimal value) even to approximate the problems MinBP-AlmostStable-sri and MinBP-AlmostStable-Max-smi within any computable function depending only on the optimal solution value.

Complementary to the optimisation problems, we denote the decision problems asking whether there exists a matching (respectively a perfect matching in the smi setting) with at most _k_ blocking pairs by _k_-BP-AlmostStable-sri and _k_-BP-AlmostStable-Perfect-smi. It is known that both of these problems are NP-complete in general, but solvable in polynomial time for a fixed parameter _k_ (i.e., in XP with respect to the fixed parameter \[20\]) \[1, 7, 8, 10\].

Glitzner and Manlove \[25\] recently studied an alternative minimax notion of almost-stability, where the maximum number of blocking pairs that any agent is contained in is minimised. They proved, for example, that even deciding whether there exists a matching in which no agent is in more than one blocking pair is NP-complete. On the positive side, they provided efficient algorithms for instances with preference lists of length at most 3, and an approximation algorithm for the sri setting.

We note that Floréen et al. \[19\] and Ostrovsky and Rosenbaum \[42\] considered other definitions of almost-stability, and almost-stable matchings have also been studied in other contexts, such as the Hospitals/Residents problem with couples \[39, 14\]. Furthermore, there is a wide literature on other solution concepts for sri instances \[29, 18, 45, 32, 46, 26, 27\].

The assumption that underlies our problem models (allowing some agents to block with each other, while disallowing other agents to block) is also related to so-called _socially-stable matchings_ and the related concept of _free edges_.

In the socially-stable matching problem (in the interpretation of \[3\]), there is an smi instance (or a many-to-one Hospitals/Residents instance), as well as a social network graph where the agents are the vertices and edges between agents indicate the social connections, and the aim is to find the largest _socially-stable_ matching, that is, the largest matching that admits no _socially-blocking pair_ (a blocking pair of agents who are connected by an edge in the social network graph). This problem is denoted by max-smiss. In our context, social stability and deviator stability coincide when the social network graph consists of every pair of (acceptable) agents that contains at least one deviator. max-smiss is known to be NP-hard even for preference lists of length at most 3 and NP-hard to approximate within some constant \[3\]. However, this<tbc>

<tbc>NP-hardness does not directly carry over to our problems, as social stability can model strictly more general blocking behaviours than our deviator stability notion.

Free edges are the direct complement of socially-blocking pairs. They are pairs of agents that are never considered to be blocking. All acceptable pairs of agents not connected in the social network graph can be considered free edges. The sri problem with free edges was first studied by Cechlárová and Fleiner [9], who proved that deciding the existence of a stable matching in the presence of free edges is NP-complete. In our context, stability with free edges and deviator stability coincide exactly when the free edges are all edges between (acceptable) conformists.

Finally, we note the (absence of a) connection between our concepts and _forced and forbidden edges_, and _critical edges and critical agents_. Forced edges are pairs of agents that must be contained in the matching, which forces a certain structure on the solutions, and forbidden edges are pairs of agents that cannot be part of the matching but can block the matching [15, 49, 48]. Neither of these notions is directly related to our model. Critical matchings match a maximum number of critical vertices, that is, vertices from a given set that should be matched as much as possible. It is easy to see that there are settings where no critical matching is stable, so a relaxed stability notion has been studied where a pair of agents that prefer each other to their partners (who may be none) is not considered blocking (despite satisfying the standard definition of a blocking pair) as long as at least one of these agents is matched to a critical vertex [36, 41]. The motivation behind this relaxed stability definition is that since maximising matched critical agents is the primary objective, we do not allow blocking pairs where one of the agents would leave a critical agent unmatched. The notion does not directly capture our model, because the motivations are different: we want to minimise the instability involving the deviator agents, possibly while maximising the overall matching size (without prioritising the number of matched deviators specifically).

Recently, Csáji et al. [13] unified the perspectives on free edges and critical relaxed stability, with the central result being a 3/2-approximation algorithm for a generalised version of max- smiss to free edges, critical vertices, and cardinal (rather than ordinal) preferences, and matroid constraints. In the same paper, the authors also introduced the concept of _free agents_, who cannot participate in any blocking pair (i.e., blocking pairs involving free agents do not cause instability). At first sight, free agents may appear to be equivalent to conformists, but this is not true, because blocking pairs involving one conformist and one deviator are possible, while one free agent and one non-free agent cannot form a blocking pair.

## 3 Deciding Deviator-Stability is Computationally Intractable

It is clear from previous work that minimising either the aggregate or the individual instability among the agents is generally intractable in a variety of critical real-world scenarios. However, generally, not every agent is able to initiate a deviation even when a beneficial opportunity to do so presents itself, for example, when they are prevented from exploring or initiating possible deviations by some external constraints. As in the introduction, we will refer to these agents as _conformists_, and to the agents that are likely to deviate as _deviators_. When the number of conformists is large, naturally, it should be easier to find a desirable matching in which the number of blocking deviators is small. In practical settings where full stability is not achievable, this might be a second-best solution. Hence, we will now introduce optimisation and decision problems that aim for matchings that give a form of preferential treatment to the deviator agents, or more generally, any designated subset of agents. Specifically, we seek matchings that minimise the number of blocking pairs involving these agents, or ideally, exclude them from any blocking pairs altogether.

We first propose the following natural optimisation problem, which seeks a matching that minimises the number of blocking pairs involving a given set of deviator agents _D_. Intuitively, the problem asks: how stable can a matching be made for a privileged subset of agents?

We will also study the maximum-cardinality matching analogue, which we define formally below.

In search of more computational tractability, we will also consider the above problem in the bipartite smi restriction, where we are given an smi instance _I_ instead, and a subset \(D\subseteq A\). We will refer to this problem as Deviator-Max-smi. Of course, all three problems are NP-hard in general, because the NP-hard problems MinBP-AlmostStable-sri and MinBP-AlmostStable-Max-smi appear as special cases when _D=A_. However, we will investigate natural restrictions and algorithms for the case when _D_ is small, and we will also show that, contrary to their non-deviator analogues, these problems turn out to be intractable even when the optimal value is 0, i.e., when merely aiming to decide whether a deviator-stable matching exists! This contrasts known complexity results as follows: deciding whether the optimal value is 0 is efficiently solvable using the Gale-Shapley or Irving’s algorithm when _D=A_, and MinBP-AlmostStable-sri is in XP with respect to the optimal parameter value, i.e., efficiently solvable for any fixed optimal parameter value \[1\].

We will first examine maximum-cardinality matchings with these properties in bipartite acceptability graphs (i.e., the Deviator-Max-smi problem) in Section 3.1, before extending our techniques to the general case in Section 3.2.

## 3.1 Deviator-Stable Maximum Matchings in Bipartite Graphs

We start by defining the following restriction of Deviator-Max-smi.

We will denote the problem of deciding whether there exists a solution to the above problem in the special case when maximum-cardinality matchings are perfect by _k_-Deviator-Perfect- smi-Dec.

Notice that whenever _D=A_ and _k_=0, then (_I,D_) is a yes-instance to 0-Deviator-Max- smi if and only if there exists a stable maximum-cardinality matching of _I_. This can be decided in polynomial time by computing a stable matching _M_ of _I_ using the Gale-Shapley algorithm \[21\] and checking whether _M_ is a maximum-cardinality matching. If it is not, then no solution exists, as every stable matching is of equal size \[43\].

Somewhat surprisingly, when \(D\subset A\), then even 0-Deviator-Perfect-smi-Dec becomes intractable, i.e., even when we merely ask whether a perfect matching exists such that no agent in _D_ is in a blocking pair.

## 4 Parametrised Algorithms

One way to cope with the strong computational intractability we established in the previous section is to explore algorithms with a parametrised time complexity. Due to Corollary 3.2, we know immediately that _k_-Deviator-Max-smi is not in the complexity class XP (and hence also not in FPT \[20\]) with respect to the maximum preference list length _d_<sub>max</sub>, assuming that \(\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}\). However, on the positive side, we will now show that the more general non-bipartite version of the problem, i.e., _k_-Deviator-Max-sri, is fixed-parameter tractable (in the complexity class FPT) with respect to the combined parameter (|_D|,d_<sub>max</sub>), as well as in XP with respect to just |_D_| (and hence the same applies also for the bipartite restriction _k_-Deviator-Max-smi). We show this by giving an algorithm, which is efficient for small sets _D_ and small _k_ or _d_<sub>max</sub> values (notice that _k_ is part of the problem, not an input parameter). Note that _d_<sub>max</sub> is naturally small in most practical scenarios: as preference lists usually need to be elicited manually, there is often a limit on how many choices a participant ranks. Indeed, we are aware of multiple real-world applications of matching schemes, such as in the allocation of students to projects, students to campus housing, or pupils to courses, where participants are asked to provide a list of their 3-8 top choices only. Furthermore, notice that when maximising the matching size as a primary objective, it is often beneficial for agents to submit a short preference list, as this may increase their chance of getting a better partner / project / room. Of course, |_D_| need not be small in general. However, one possible strategy is to fix _k_=0, in which case the algorithm terminates in \(O(d_\mathrm{max}^{O(|D|)}n^{5/2})\) time, and rank agents based on their likelihood to deviate. Then, one could start by including only the strongest deviators in _D_, in which case _D_ is small, and iteratively increase the size of _D_ up until either no more solution exists in which no deviator agent is blocking, or the computation takes too long.

## 5 Minimising the Number of Blocking Deviators Instead

As discussed in Section 2.2, an alternative approach to minimising blocking pairs is to minimise the number of blocking agents. There is an inherent trade-off: minimising blocking pairs minimises the aggregate instability of the matching, but might involve a higher total number of blocking agents that have an individual incentive to deviate. Minimising blocking agents instead aims to give as few agents as possible an incentive to deviate, although their individual incentives or opportunities to deviate might be higher due to possibly more blocking pairs that they are a part of. As a third option, minimax almost-stable matchings, which were recently investigated by Glitzner and Manlove \[25\], minimise the maximum individual incentive to deviate.

In this section, we will briefly highlight that minimising the number of blocking deviators remains NP-hard. However, we will also show how to extend the FPT algorithms to this setting. Let Deviator-BA-sri and Deviator-BA-Max-sri denote versions of Deviator-sri and Deviator-Max-sri that minimise \(|\{a_i\in D|bp_{a_i}(M)\neq\varnothing\}|\) among all matchings and all maximum-cardinality matchings, respectively. Furthermore, let _k_-Deviator-BA-sri and _k_-Deviator-BA-Max-sri denote the problems of computing a matching and a maximum- cardinality matching admitting at most _k_ blocking agents in _D_, if they exist, respectively. Also, let 0-Deviator-BA-sri-Dec and 0-Deviator-BA-Perfect-smi-Dec denote the restricted problems of deciding whether such a solution exists when _k_=0 and, in the smi case, where maximum-cardinality matchings are perfect, and the instance is bipartite. We can immediately conclude the following.

**Theorem 5.1.** 0-Deviator-BA-sri-Dec _is_ NP-complete_, regardless of whether preference lists are of length at most 5 or complete._ 0-Deviator-BA-Perfect-smi-Dec _is_ NP-complete_, even if all preference lists are of length at most 3 and all deviators are on the same side._

_Proof._ Clearly, both problems are in NP: we can easily check a possible solution _M_ by iterating through the set of deviator agents and checking that none of them block with any agent that they prefer to their partner in _M_ (which might be none). For the Perfect-smi case, we furthermore need to check that every agent in the instance has a partner in _M_, which can be done efficiently by iterating through the set of agents once.

Now, let \(I=(A,\succ)\) be an sri instance and let \(D\subseteq A\). Then there exists a matching \(M\in\mathcal{M}\) such that \(|\{a_i\in D|bp_{a_i}(M)\neq\varnothing\}|=0\) if and only if \(\bigcup_{a_i\in D}bp_{a_i}(M)=\varnothing\). Hence, (_I,D_) is a yes-instance to 0-Deviator-BA-sri-Dec if and only if it is a yes-instance to 0- Deviator-sri-Dec, which we showed to be NP-complete regardless of whether preference lists are of length at most 5 or complete in Theorem 3.5.

Similarly, let \(I=(A,\succ)\) be an smi instance and let \(D\subseteq A\). Then there exists a matching \(M\in\mathcal{M}^+\) such that \(|\{a_i\in D|bp_{a_i}(M)\neq\varnothing\}|=0\) if and only if \(\bigcup_{a_i\in D}bp_{a_i}(M)=\varnothing\). Hence, (_I,D_) is a yes-instance to 0-Deviator-BA-Perfect-smi-Dec if and only if it is a yes-instance to 0-Deviator-Perfect-smi-Dec, which we showed to be NP-complete even in the case where preference lists are of length at most 3 and all deviators are on the same side in Theorem 3.1.

Thus, we can immediately conclude the following intractability results for our desired optimisation problems.

**Corollary 5.2.** Deviator-BA-sri _and_ Deviator-BA-Max-smi _are_ NP-hard _and are not in_ XP _(unless_ P=NP_) with respect to optimum values_ \(\kappa=min_{M\in\mathcal{M}}|\{a_i\in D|bp_{a_i}(M)\neq\varnothing\}|\) _and_ \(\kappa=min_{M\in\mathcal{M}^+}|\{a_i\in D|bp_{a_i}(M)\neq\varnothing\}|\)_, respectively._

## 7 Resolving Further Open Cases

When aggregating an overview of known and newly established complexity results in  1 (to follow in Section 8), we identified two further cases that, to the best of our knowledge, have not yet been detailed explicitly in existing literature. Both concern the minimisation of blocking agents in sri across the whole instance, i.e., the MinBA-AlmostStable-sri problem, which is also the special case of Deviator-BA-sri where _D=A_. It is known that MinBA- AlmostStable-sri is NP-hard when preference lists are of length 5 \[11\].

The first result shows that when preference lists are very short, then MinBA-AlmostStable- sri is solvable in polynomial time. This follows immediately from our algorithm in Section 6.

**Theorem 7.1.** MinBA-AlmostStable-sri _can be solved in O(n_) _time when preference lists are of length at most 2 (where n is the number of agents)._

_Proof._ We already noted above that MinBA-AlmostStable-sri is the special case of the problem Deviator-BA-sri where all agents are part of the deviator set. Therefore, due to Theorem 6.1, Algorithm 2 solves MinBA-AlmostStable-sri to optimality in, asymptotically, at most linear time in the number of agents.

The second result shows that MinBA-AlmostStable-sri remains intractable even when preference lists are complete.

## 8 Conclusion

In this paper, we considered a simple premise: some agents can initiate blocking pair-based deviations, and some agents cannot. We aimed to answer the following question from a computational complexity point of view: Can we find desirable matchings in which no deviator is incentivised to deviate? The short answer is yes, but only under strong assumptions on the input. Our key insights are summarised in  1 and reveal a sharp contrast between strong intractability and tractable special cases.

We conclude with a number of open questions. For instance, on the parametrised complexity front, are the problems Deviator-sri and Deviator-Max-sri in FPT with respect to just |_D_|, rather than the combined parameter (|_D|,d_<sub>max</sub>)? We conjecture that the answer is no, as it might be the case that \(|D|\checkmark d_\mathrm{max}\), but our current reductions rely on the fact that _D_ is sufficiently large. It would also be interesting to study approximation algorithms in the setting of deviator stability, although we highlight that strong inapproximability results for almost- stable matchings are known \[1, 8, 12\] and that we proved that even deciding whether there exists a matching where no deviator is blocking is NP-complete. Thus, it might be interesting to study algorithms that give guarantees with respect to the number of deviators that are in no or in few blocking pairs, while ignoring the remaining deviators. Lastly, on a more practical front, it would be interesting to design, deploy and study real-world multi-agent systems using deviator-stable matchings - how do we accurately identify deviators in practice, and are there sufficiently few to render our parametrised algorithms efficient?
